Skip next section India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up 09/19/2026 September 19, 2026 India swaps flagbearer for Asian Games opening ceremony after kit mix-up Toor is aiming to bring home his third gold medal at the Asian Games Image: David J. Phillip/AP Photo/picture alliance A last-minute logistics problem has cost shot-putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor his spot as India's male flagbearer at Saturday's Asian Games opening ceremony in Nagoya, Japan. Kabaddi player Pawan Sehrawat is set to step in instead, joining shooter Manu Bhaker, a two-time Paris Olympics bronze medalist, who will be India's female flagbearer. Toor, who is chasing a third consecutive Asian Games gold in shot put, said he only learned of his selection as flagbearer a day earlier and that his kit was still back in India. "I'm told that my kit will reach at 3 p.m. at the airport. Reaching the opening ceremony venue after collecting my kit from the airport on time will be very difficult," he told news agency PTI, adding that he had informed the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) that he would not be attending the ceremony. The Indian Olympic Association said in a statement that Toor would be unable to serve as flagbearer "due to a technical issue." The mix-up was one of several hiccups in the run-up to the Games, which open on Saturday with more than 17,000 athletes competing across more than 40 sports through October 4. Organizers, working without a traditional athletes' village, have housed competitors in container-style huts, hotels and a cruise ship. There have been complaints over accommodation quality, transport delays, and a mistaken playing of North Korea's national anthem for South Korea's men's hockey team. A tropical storm bearing down on the region threatens to cause further disruption as competition gets underway. The lack of a traditional village has led to athletes being housed in makeshift huts Image: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS https://p.dw.com/p/5Mstp Skip next section Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody 09/19/2026 September 19, 2026 Delhi High Court grants bail to Jagtar Singh Johal after nearly nine years in custody The Delhi High Court granted bail to British national Jagtar Singh Johal in seven murder and terrorism-related cases, clearing the way for his conditional release after nearly nine years in Indian custody. The court overturned a 2024 ruling that had denied him bail. Johal, 39, a Sikh rights campaigner from Dumbarton, Scotland, was arrested in Punjab in 2017 shortly after he arrived in India for his wedding. He was accused by India's National Investigation Agency of financing and courier work for the banned Khalistan Liberation Force in connection with a series of targeted killings in Ludhiana and Jalandhar districts between 2016 and 2017. He was acquitted in a related case last year by a court in Moga, Punjab, while the Delhi cases had continued. Johal has consistently denied wrongdoing and says he was tortured into signing a false confession. A United Nations working group ruled in May 2022 that his detention was arbitrary. "Eight and a half years of arbitrary detention without a clear path to trial is not justice, it is unlawful suffering," UN human rights experts said in a statement earlier this year. "The prolonged uncertainty alone is a form of psychological torture." Indian authorities have repeatedly rejected the torture allegations and insisted that due process was followed. What did the court say in its ruling? In its ruling, the court cited Johal's prolonged incarceration and the slow pace of the trial as grounds for bail, despite the strict conditions typically imposed under India's anti-terror law, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The court noted that 123 witnesses were yet to be examined and that proceedings were "certainly not likely to conclude any time soon." The court imposed strict bail conditions, including surrendering his passport, restrictions on communication and social media activity, and regular reporting to the Investigating Officer. The court did not rule on the merits of the underlying case, leaving prosecutors free to have his bail revoked if the conditions of his release are breached. Johal's brother, Gurpreet Singh Johal, who has campaigned for years for his release and urged successive UK governments to take action, called the ruling "a huge relief," the BBC reported. "I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison." https://www.politico.eu/article/helen-wh.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — One of Kemi Badenoch’s most senior frontbench colleagues has branded Andy Burnham’s conference speech last week as “absolutely mad.” Speaking to POLITICO, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, argued that a “very different view of the country” will become clear at the Conservative Party conference this week. “I see Andy Burnham saying, look, if we just hope hard enough, everything will be fine, and let’s achieve growth by taxing more and spending more, and more public ownership and more regulation,” she said. “To me, as a Conservative, that is absolutely mad. That is how you make our economy worse, and that is how you make people poorer.” Advertisement Advertisement Her fierce attack on Burnham’s speech reveals a more combative approach from Badenoch and her shadow cabinet as the conference in Birmingham gets underway. Whately accused the prime minister of having the “wrong political philosophy and understanding of the economy.” She left little wriggle room when she defended the party’s approach to the triple lock, a state pension increase guarantee introduced by the Tories — and now being tweaked by Burnham to fund a social care overhaul. Over the weekend, Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Conservatives would commit to the triple lock “for this parliament” — without making an express pledge to keep it in the party’s next manifesto. But the shadow work and pensions struck a more defiant tone. “Kemi is absolutely dead clear about it,” Whately insisted in her POLITICO interview. “The triple lock is Conservative policy. The answer to the problems that our country faces isn’t to go after pensioners. The answer is to get people working, and the core to my brief is to make savings from the welfare bill where we’ve got seven million people of working age on out-of-work benefits. Let’s get some of those seven million people into work.” Childcare drive Whately also defended the Conservative Party’s pledge to offer free childcare to parents earning over £100,000. The current “cliff edge” means parents in England lose out on tens of thousands of pounds of childcare support when they reach this income. The former Conservative MP Miriam Cates has questioned whether the policy might harm support for parents who want to stay at home rather than get back into the workplace as soon as possible, and risks treating them as “economic units.” Advertisement Advertisement But Whately said: “I’ve had those arguments sometimes with colleagues, Miriam included, about whether we should be doing the kind of policies that some other countries do. I think Hungary was the obvious example of more paying people to essentially have children. Those are things are incredibly expensive. We’re not going down that route.” “What we have to do is we have to make sure that our tax system supports growth, supports the economy,” she added. Whately vowed that the Conservatives would meanwhile clamp down on access to working-age benefits. “The way that we are assessing people for access to sickness benefits is very flawed,” she said. “A huge amount of assessments are done over the phone, just with forms, people not being seen in person… it means that those who really are sick are now having to sort of compete with all the benefits of those who have seen on the internet how they can most effectively make sure they maximize their claim.” Pressed on whether the party’s opponents could seize on policies curbing access to social security — as has happened to the Trump administration in the U.S. as it clamped down on programs like food assistance — Whately said: “This is specifically about people who could and should be working. It isn’t a policy about people who have disabilities and who are on the Universal Credit health component.” Whately was also pressed on her former friendship with Robert Jenrick, a one-time Conservative leadership contender who has defected to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. The Tory conference center this year boasts a spoof Bayeux Tapestry on prominent display — which includes several images of Jenrick, the former shadow justice secretary. Whately and Jenrick were close colleagues until his switch to Reform earlier this year. “I’m not feeling like we’re missing him right now,” Whately said. “I considered Rob a friend, and now he’s not a friend in my life … because of the way he behaved, and because he lied to people and deceived people.” Hear the full the interview on the Politics at Sam and Anne’s podcast.
